a: Ignatius, also called Theophorus
p: Every letter opens with his second name, Theophorus, 'God-bearer'.
b: Greek Ignatios, ho kai Theophoros, 'Ignatius, who is also Theophorus'. The second name is built from theos, 'God', and pherō, 'carry'. Lake's footnote gives 'The God-bearer' and a story from the third-century Acts of Ignatius: the emperor asks, 'And who is Theophorus?' and Ignatius answers, 'He who has Christ in his heart.' The Orthodox Church in America gives the same meaning, 'because he bore God in his heart', and adds a tradition that he was the child Christ held in his arms. Ignatius plays on the name in 9:2, where he calls the Ephesians 'God-bearers'.
orig: Ἰγνάτιος, ὁ καὶ Θεοφόρος (Ignatios, ho kai Theophoros)

a: the church in Ephesus of Asia
t: Ephesus, a church with a long history
p: The great port of the Roman province of Asia, where Paul had worked for years.
b: Ephesus was the chief city of the Roman province called Asia, on the west coast of what is now Turkey. Paul stayed there more than two years (Acts 19:10) and later called its elders to Miletus (Acts 20:17), and the first of the seven letters in Revelation goes to its church (Revelation 2:1-7). Ignatius writes to it from Smyrna, up the coast to the north (21:1). He knows its fame: it is 'a church famous through the ages' (8:1), and its Christians 'have always agreed with the apostles' (11:2).

a: Jesus Christ our God
p: Ignatius calls Jesus 'God' without hedging, here and many times after.
b: Greek Iēsou Christou tou theou hēmōn, 'Jesus Christ, our God'. Ignatius calls Jesus God again and again: 'the blood of God' (1:1), 'God in man' (7:2), 'our God, Jesus the Christ' (18:2), 'God was made known in a human way' (19:3). He also prays to 'the Father' and speaks of Jesus as 'his Son' (4:2), so he does not mean that Jesus is the Father. The Plain English Translation keeps every one of these as Ignatius wrote it. The New Testament has a few places that may call Jesus God, and they are debated: 'My Lord and my God!' (John 20:28); 'our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ' (Titus 2:13; see the card there); 'God blessed forever' (Romans 9:5). Ignatius, writing a few decades later, says it plainly.
orig: Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν (Iēsou Christou tou theou hēmōn)

a: Before the ages it was marked out ahead of time
p: The greeting is full of words from Paul's letter to the same church.
b: Ignatius stacks up titles for the church, as Paul did when he wrote to Ephesus: 'blessed', 'marked out ahead of time' (Greek proōrismenē, the verb of Ephesians 1:5 and 1:11), 'chosen' (Ephesians 1:4), 'the fullness' (Greek plērōma, Ephesians 1:23), 'glory' (Ephesians 1:6, 12, 14). Whether Ignatius had Paul's letter in front of him is not something the greeting can prove, but he says in 12:2 that Paul remembers the Ephesians 'in every letter'.

a: the blood of God
p: A bold phrase: the one who bled on the cross is God.
b: Greek en haimati theou, 'in the blood of God'. Ignatius means Christ's blood shed on the cross, and he does not soften it to 'the blood of Christ'. The closest New Testament wording is Paul's speech to the elders of this same city, Ephesus: 'the church of God, which he acquired through his own blood' (Acts 20:28), a verse whose wording also differs between manuscripts. Later writers argued over whether God can be said to suffer; Ignatius's answer comes in 7:2, 'first able to suffer and then beyond suffering'.

a: rekindled
p: The same verb Paul uses for Timothy's gift, 'stir up the fire'.
b: Greek anazōpyrēsantes, 'having rekindled', from a word for blowing on coals to make them flame up again (LSJ). It is the verb of 2 Timothy 1:6: 'stir up the fire of God's gift again'. Its object here is 'the work' (Lake: 'having kindled your brotherly task'): by the blood of God the Ephesians fanned their kindness into flame again, and showed it when they sent their overseer and others to meet Ignatius (1:3-2:1).

a: the work that comes naturally to you
p: Greek syngenikon: inborn, natural, or 'brotherly'. Translators differ.
b: Greek to syngenikon ergon. The adjective means 'inborn, natural' and also 'of or for kinsmen' (LSJ). Lake translates 'your brotherly task', and his footnote says this is Zahn's rendering, while Lightfoot suggested 'natural' or 'congenial'. The Plain English Translation takes the first sense: kindness to a stranger in chains is the kind of work that comes naturally to people who are 'imitators of God'.

a: imitators of God
p: Paul told the Ephesians the same: 'become imitators of God'.
b: Greek mimētai ontes theou. Paul's letter to Ephesus says, 'So become imitators of God, like children who are loved' (Ephesians 5:1). Imitation is one of Ignatius's great themes: 'Let us be eager to be imitators of the Lord' (10:3), and in his letter to Rome he asks to be 'an imitator of the suffering of my God' (Ignatius to the Romans 6:3).

a: on my way from Syria in chains
p: Ignatius was being taken under guard from Antioch in Syria to Rome.
b: Greek dedemenon apo Syrias, 'bound from Syria'. Eusebius tells the story: Ignatius, overseer of Antioch, was 'sent from Syria to Rome, and became food for wild beasts on account of his testimony to Christ', and he traveled 'through Asia under the strictest military surveillance' (Church History 3.36.3-4). In his letter to Rome Ignatius calls his guards 'ten leopards' (Ignatius to the Romans 5:1). He was in Smyrna when he wrote this letter (21:1).

a: to reach the goal of fighting wild beasts in Rome
p: Condemned people were thrown to animals in the arena as public entertainment.
b: Greek thēriomachēsai, 'to fight wild beasts', the word of 1 Corinthians 15:32, 'I fought with wild beasts at Ephesus', which may be a figure for Paul's dangers there. For Ignatius it is literal: at the games, condemned prisoners were killed by animals. He does not dread it. He 'hopes' to reach it, because by it he will be 'a disciple'. Jerome reports that he 'was put to death the eleventh year of Trajan' (Lives of Illustrious Men 16); Lake gives Eusebius's date, 'the tenth year of Trajan, i.e. 108 A.D.', and says modern critics are 'by no means unanimous' about it.

a: so that by reaching it I may be able to be a disciple
t: Only a disciple at the end?
p: Ignatius thinks of martyrdom as the moment he becomes a true disciple.
b: Greek hina dia tou epitychein dynēthō mathētēs einai. Ignatius says the same in 3:1 ('I have only made a start at being a disciple') and in Ignatius to the Romans 5:3. He does not deny that he is already a believer; he takes Jesus at his word: 'Anyone who does not carry his own cross and come behind me cannot be a disciple of mine' (Luke 14:27). Lake notes that the letter to Rome was written to keep Christians there from trying to save him and so 'robbing him of the crown of martyrdom'. The longing echoes Paul: 'For me, living is Christ and dying is gain' (Philippians 1:21).

a: Onesimus
p: The leader of the Ephesian church, who came to Smyrna to meet Ignatius.
b: Eusebius says that in this letter Ignatius 'mentions Onesimus, its pastor' (Church History 3.36.5). Lightfoot names him with Polycarp as one of 'two bishops' the letters mention, and adds, 'of the former nothing more is known' (The Christian Ministry, pages 48-49). The name means 'useful' and was common among slaves. Whether he is the runaway slave of Philemon, for whom Paul pleaded some fifty years earlier (Philemon 1:10), is a question the site's topic page on Onesimus takes up.

a: I have received your whole large community
t: The whole church in one man
p: Ignatius says he has met the whole church in its overseer.
b: Greek tēn polyplētheian hymōn ... apeilēpha en Onēsimō, 'I have received your great multitude in Onesimus'. The overseer stands for the church. Ignatius says the same of the others in 2:1: 'Through them I have seen all of you in love.' Lightfoot quotes this verse as an example of what Ignatius valued in the overseer: a visible 'centre of unity' (The Christian Ministry, pages 84-85).
orig: τὴν πολυπλήθειαν ὑμῶν ... ἀπείληφα (tēn polyplētheian hymōn ... apeilēpha)

a: my fellow slave Burrhus
p: Ignatius calls the Ephesian deacon Burrhus his fellow slave of Christ.
b: Greek tou syndoulou mou Bourrou. 'Fellow slave' is Paul's word for co-workers: Epaphras is 'our beloved fellow slave' (Colossians 1:7). Ignatius uses it of deacons in his other letters too: Lake's English has 'my fellow servant the deacon Zotion' in To the Magnesians 2 and 'the deacons my fellow servants' in To the Philadelphians 4. Burrhus is 'your deacon', Greek diakonos, as in Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3:8. Ignatius asks that he 'stay on with me' (Greek paramenein, 'remain beside'), and he did: the letters to the Philadelphians and Smyrnaeans, written later from Troas, say they were written through Burrhus (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:1).
orig: τοῦ συνδούλου μου Βούρρου (tou syndoulou mou Bourrou)

a: Crocus
p: Men of the Ephesian church known only from this letter.
b: Crocus, Euplus and Fronto are otherwise unknown. With Onesimus and Burrhus they made up the party the Ephesians sent to Smyrna to greet Ignatius (21:1). Lake says the purpose of this and most of the letters is 'to thank the recipients for the kindness which they had shown to Ignatius'. Crocus is 'a living sample of your love': the Greek exemplarion is a Latin loanword, exemplarium, 'a copy, a model'.

a: May I always have the benefit of you
t: 'May I have the benefit of you': Philemon's verb
p: Right after naming Onesimus, Ignatius uses the rare verb of Paul's play on that name.
b: Greek onaimēn hymōn dia pantos. The verb onaimēn, 'may I have benefit', is the one Paul uses in Philemon, the letter about the slave Onesimus, whose name means 'useful': 'Yes, brother, let me gain something from you in the Lord. Set my heart at rest in Christ.' (Philemon 1:20). Ignatius has just named Onesimus, the Ephesians' overseer (1:3; 2:1), and in the same breath said that Crocus 'has refreshed me in every way' (2:1, Greek anepausen), the verb Philemon 1:7 and 1:20 use for hearts 'set at rest'. Lake's English, 'May I ever have joy of you', gives the sense; the Plain English Translation keeps the verb's own meaning so the echo can be seen. These are facts of the Greek. Whether they mean that Ignatius had Paul's letter and its Onesimus in mind, or that the two men are one, is a further question: see the topic page Onesimus.
orig: ὀναίμην ὑμῶν διὰ παντός (onaimēn hymōn dia pantos)

a: submitting to the overseer and the council of elders
p: One overseer with a council of elders around him: Ignatius's church order.
b: Greek tō episkopō kai tō presbyteriō. Episkopos, 'overseer', is the word behind 'bishop'; presbyterion, 'council of elders', is the word of 1 Timothy 4:14 ('the elders' hands'). In Ignatius there is one overseer in each church, with elders and deacons under him (the three named together, Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1). In the New Testament the words 'overseer' and 'elder' often name one office (Acts 20:17 with Acts 20:28; Titus 1:5-7). How the one became the other is one of the great questions of church history; see the note at 6:1 and chapter 5's page.
orig: τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ καὶ τῷ πρεσβυτερίῳ (tō episkopō kai tō presbyteriō)

a: rub me down with oil
p: A picture from the gym: an athlete was rubbed with oil before a fight.
b: Greek hypaleiphthēnai, 'to be anointed'. Lake's footnote: 'Literally "anointed." The allusion is to the preparation of a gymnast or gladiator.' LSJ gives the same verb for one who 'anoints himself to fight'. Ignatius, going to the arena, asks the Ephesians to prepare him like a trainer, but their oil is faith, warning, endurance and patience. He uses the athlete picture often; Paul does too (1 Corinthians 9:24-27).

a: bound in the Name
p: Christians in the early church often said simply 'the Name' for Jesus' name.
b: Greek en tō onomati, 'in the name'. The absolute use is old: the apostles were glad 'because they had been found worthy to be dishonored for the sake of the Name' (Acts 5:41), and of the missionaries, 'It was for the sake of the Name that they set out' (3 John 7). Ignatius uses it the same way in 1:2 ('the name ... we share') and 7:1 ('carrying the Name around').

a: the overseers who are appointed throughout the ends of the earth
t: Overseers throughout the ends of the earth
p: Ignatius assumes there are overseers in churches everywhere.
b: Greek hoi episkopoi, hoi kata ta perata horisthentes. Ignatius takes it for granted that churches 'throughout the ends of the earth' are led by an overseer. The Greek kata ta perata is 'throughout the farthest parts', and Lightfoot gives the phrase as 'established in the farthest parts of the world' (page 86): the overseers are not sent out to the ends of the earth but are found there. Lightfoot quotes the phrase among the Greek letters' 'far stronger expressions' for the office, and says that 'throughout the whole range of Christian literature, no more uncompromising advocacy of the episcopate can be found' (The Christian Ministry, pages 85-86). Whether every church of his time really had one overseer is another matter: Polycarp's letter to Philippi names only 'elders and deacons' there (Polycarp to the Philippians 5:3). See chapter 5's page.
orig: οἱ κατὰ τὰ πέρατα ὁρισθέντες (hoi kata ta perata horisthentes)

a: run together with the mind of God
p: The Greek pictures a church running side by side with God's purpose.
b: Greek syntrechēte tē gnōmē tou theou. Lake's footnote: 'Literally "run".' Gnōmē is a mind, a purpose, a will. The thought runs in a chain: the church runs with God's mind; Jesus Christ is the Father's mind; the overseers are in Jesus Christ's mind; so the Ephesians run with their overseer's mind (4:1).

a: as strings are to a lyre
p: The overseer is the lyre; the elders are the strings; the church is the choir.
b: Greek hōs chordai kithara. Ignatius turns church order into music. The council of elders is tuned to the overseer like strings to a lyre; in 4:2 every member joins the choir and takes 'God's pitch' (Greek chrōma; Lake's footnote: 'key ... in the musical sense'); and the song is Jesus Christ himself: 'Jesus Christ is sung'. The picture of unity is harmony, not sameness: many voices, one song. Lightfoot quotes the lyre among Ignatius's pictures of the elders around the overseer (The Christian Ministry, page 87).

a: members of his Son
p: Paul's picture of the church as Christ's body.
b: Greek melē ... tou huiou autou. Paul told the Corinthians, 'Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a part of it' (1 Corinthians 12:27), and the Ephesians that 'the church is his body' (Ephesians 1:23). Ignatius joins it to his music: the Father hears the one song and knows the singers as limbs of his Son.
orig: μέλη ὄντας τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ (melē ontas tou huiou autou)

a: within the altar
p: The altar here is the place of the church's gathering, or the church itself.
b: Greek entos tou thysiastēriou. Lake translates 'within the sanctuary'. In the Greek Old Testament the word is the altar of the tabernacle and the Temple. Ignatius uses it of the church. In Lake's English of To the Trallians 7, 'He who is within the sanctuary is pure', which means that 'whoever does anything apart from the bishop and the presbytery and the deacons is not pure'; and To the Philadelphians 4 has 'one altar, as there is one bishop'. So the altar is bound up with the gathered church and its leaders. Whether Ignatius also means the table of the Supper is read differently by different churches. Hebrews 13:10 already says, 'We have an altar'.

a: God's bread
p: The same words as John 6:33, which Lake prints in the margin.
b: Greek tou artou tou theou, as in John 6:33, which Lake prints in the margin: "God's bread is what comes down out of heaven and gives the world life." (John 6:33). Whoever cuts himself off from the church's gathering 'goes without' it. Whether the bread here is the bread of the Lord's Supper, or Christ received by faith in the common life, is read differently by different churches; see the note at 20:2 and the cards at John 6 and Matthew 26.
orig: τοῦ ἄρτου τοῦ θεοῦ (tou artou tou theou)

a: the prayer of one or two
t: The prayer of one or two
p: An echo of Jesus' promise to two or three gathered in his name.
b: Ignatius argues from small to great: if the prayer of 'one or two' is strong, how much more the prayer of the whole church with its overseer. The picture is close to Jesus' saying, 'For wherever two or three have come together in my name, I am right there in the middle of them' (Matthew 18:20), with the verse before it on two who agree in prayer (Matthew 18:19). The Catholic Encyclopedia lists 'the value of united prayer' among the teachings it finds in this letter (at 13:1).

a: For it is written
p: Ignatius's only quotation with a formula in this letter, in James and 1 Peter's form.
b: The one place in the letter where Ignatius says 'it is written' (Greek gegraptai). The verse is Proverbs 3:34 as the Greek Bible has it, in the form James and 1 Peter quote: 'God takes his stand against the proud, but to the humble he gives grace' (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5), with 'God' where the Greek Proverbs has 'the Lord'. The site's Proverbs 3:34, made from the Hebrew, reads differently ('Mockers he mocks'), so the Plain English Translation follows the site's James 4:6. Ignatius then plays on the verb: God 'takes his stand against' the proud, so 'let us be eager not to take a stand against the overseer'.

a: does not gather in one place
p: Greek epi to auto, 'to the same place': the phrase for the church's meeting.
b: Greek ho mē erchomenos epi to auto. The phrase means 'together, in one place', and Acts uses it for the first believers: 'All who believed kept together' (Acts 2:44). Ignatius uses it again in 13:1 ('when you gather in one place often'), and the Plain English Translation gives it the same words in both verses. Lake's footnote points out 'a curious mixture of tenses': Ignatius may have a real case in mind.

a: keeping silent
p: Ignatius defends an overseer who says little.
b: Greek sigōnta episkopon. Some at Ephesus seem to have thought little of their overseer because he was quiet. Ignatius turns the charge around: silence is godly. In 15:1-2 he says that the one Teacher 'spoke, and it came to be', and that what he did 'in silence is worthy of the Father', and in 19:1 that God's great mysteries were done 'in God's quiet'. He defends the overseer of Philadelphia the same way: in Lake's English of To the Philadelphians 1, 'I was amazed ... at his ability to do more by silence than those who use vain words.' The Plain English Translation keeps 'silent' and 'quiet' as separate words, as the Greek does.

a: we must receive just like the one who sent him
p: An echo of Jesus' saying that whoever receives his messenger receives him.
b: The rule of the ancient world was that a messenger stood for his master. Jesus used it: 'whoever takes in someone I send takes me in, and whoever takes me in takes in the one who sent me' (John 13:20; compare Matthew 10:40). Ignatius applies it to the overseer, sent by 'the master of the house' to manage his household (Greek oikonomia; compare the steward of Luke 12:42).

a: look at the overseer as at the Lord himself
p: One of Ignatius's strongest lines on the overseer, read in very different ways.
b:
Greek ton episkopon ... hōs auton ton kyrion dei prosblepein. The churches read this line, and Ignatius's teaching on the overseer, very differently.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church takes up Ignatius's picture of the bishop: 'he is like the living image of God the Father' (paragraph 1549, citing To the Trallians 3:1 and To the Magnesians 6:1). The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) cites this chapter for the teaching that 'the hierarchy of the Church was instituted by Christ'. Lightfoot, an Anglican bishop, held that the office grew 'out of the presbyteral by elevation', first in the regions where the last apostles lived and not apart from 'their influence or their sanction'; he wrote that this language, 'if taken literally', would give the overseer 'crushing despotism', and explained it by 'the needs and distractions of the age' (The Christian Ministry, pages 24-25, 73, 87-88). Calvin rejected the writings under Ignatius's name altogether, though the Ignatius he knew was the long, interpolated form (see the book's pages). Chapter 5's page gives these readings more fully, and the site's cards at Acts 20:28 and 1 Timothy 3 give each church's teaching on overseers and elders.

a: no heresy makes its home among you
p: Greek hairesis: first a 'choice' or 'party', here a group with false teaching.
b: Greek hairesis, from a verb 'to choose'. In Acts the word names a party without blame: 'the Pharisees' party' (Acts 15:5), 'the sect of the Nazarenes' (Acts 24:5). Paul lists 'factions' among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:20), and 2 Peter 2:1 warns of false teachers who 'sneak in factions that bring ruin'. Ignatius uses it of teaching that splits a church from its overseer and from the truth about Christ. Eusebius says he warned the churches 'against the heresies that were then beginning to prevail' (Church History 3.36.4).

a: rabid dogs that bite on the sly
t: Mad dogs and the one doctor
p: False teachers are like rabid dogs whose bite is hard to heal.
b: Greek kynes lyssōntes, lathrodēktai, 'raging dogs, secret biters', and dystherapeutous, 'hard to cure'. 'Dogs' is an old word of contempt for enemies of the faith (Philippians 3:2; Revelation 22:15). The words 'hard to heal' set up the next verse: against the bite there is only 'one doctor'. Ignatius does not name the false teachers, but 7:2 shows what they denied: that Christ really came in the flesh and really suffered (see the topic Docetism and the notes at 18:2-19:3).

a: There is one doctor
p: Jesus as doctor: the picture of the Gospels, turned into a hymn.
b: Greek heis iatros estin. Jesus called himself a doctor: 'People who are strong do not need a doctor. Sick people do' (Mark 2:17). Ignatius builds on the picture: the false teaching is a bite that is 'hard to heal' (7:1), and the cure is Christ, whose bread is 'the medicine of immortality' (20:2). The rest of the verse is a chain of pairs, flesh and spirit, born and unborn, God and man, death and life, Mary and God, suffering and beyond suffering. It has the balanced shape of a hymn or creed. The line breaks in the Plain English Translation show the pairs.

a: born and unborn
p: Greek gennētos kai agennētos: born of Mary, yet without beginning as God.
b: Greek gennētos kai agennētos, from the verb for being born: Christ is 'born' as a man, and 'unborn' as God (Lake: 'born and yet not born'). Two hundred years later the words mattered in the arguments over Arius, who said the Son had a beginning, and Athanasius quoted this verse in his book on the councils. His Greek, as Migne prints it, has a different spelling: genētos kai agenētos, with one n, so 'originate and unoriginate' in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers English, and 'made and not made' in the Latin printed beside it. The editors' note there records the double n in one manuscript of Athanasius and judges the single n to be his own reading, as what follows shows; another of their notes says that Athanasius confuses the two words. What follows is his explanation: Ignatius called Christ originate 'on account of the flesh (for He became flesh)', yet unoriginate, 'because He is not in the number of things made' (On the Councils 47). So the line as Athanasius used it is about being made, where Lake's text is about being born. Lake prints the double n without a footnote, and the site has opened no source that settles which spelling Ignatius wrote.

a: first able to suffer and then beyond suffering
t: Able to suffer, then beyond suffering
p: Christ truly suffered in the flesh, and after the resurrection he cannot suffer.
b: Greek prōton pathētos kai tote apathēs. The phrase answers the false teachers who said Christ only seemed to suffer (the view later called docetism, from Greek dokein, 'to seem'; Lake's introduction says the letters protest 'against the form of heresy called docetism'). For Ignatius the order is everything: first real suffering, then the risen life. The same chain runs in 1 Timothy 3:16, 'He was made visible in the flesh, proven right in the Spirit', and in Romans 1:3-4.
orig: πρῶτον παθητὸς καὶ τότε ἀπαθής (prōton pathētos kai tote apathēs)

a: I am the lowliest of your servants
p: Greek peripsēma: literally 'scrapings', a picture of the lowest thing.
b: Greek peripsēma hymōn, 'your scrapings'. The word means 'anything wiped off', and it is the word of 1 Corinthians 4:13, 'the garbage of everything'. Lake's footnote says it was used 'of criminals and others whose death was regarded as a piacular sacrifice', and 'ultimately ... became merely a form of epistolary politeness'. LSJ lists it as a polite formula in inscriptions, 'your humble servant'. The Epistle of Barnabas uses it the same way (Barnabas 4:9). With it Ignatius says hagnizomai hymōn, 'I am purified for you' or 'I devote myself for you': he gives his coming death as an offering for them. He repeats the word in 18:1.
orig: περίψημα ὑμῶν καὶ ἁγνίζομαι ὑμῶν (peripsēma hymōn kai hagnizomai hymōn)

a: People of the flesh cannot do the things of the spirit
p: Paul's contrast of flesh and Spirit, with a twist at the end.
b: Lake's margin points to Romans 8: 'People who live by the flesh have their minds on the things of the flesh' (Romans 8:5), and 'People who are in the flesh cannot please God' (Romans 8:8). Then Ignatius adds something Paul did not say in so many words: 'even what you do in the flesh is spiritual, for you do everything in Jesus Christ.' Ordinary bodily life, lived in Christ, is holy. 'Flesh and spirit' run all through the letter (7:2; 10:3).

a: some people from over there
p: Wandering teachers moved from church to church along the roads of Asia.
b: Greek parodeusantas tinas ekeithen, 'some who passed through from there'. Ignatius does not say where 'there' was. Traveling teachers were a real problem for the early churches: 'do not take him into the house' (2 John 10), and the Didache gives rules for testing traveling apostles and prophets (Didache 11:1-6). Ephesus was a great crossroads, and these teachers 'passed through' without being let in.

a: the crane of Jesus Christ, which is the cross
t: The cross as a building crane
p: Living stones hoisted into God's temple by the cross, with the Spirit as the rope.
b:
Greek dia tēs mēchanēs Iēsou Christou, hos estin stauros, schoiniō chrōmenoi tō pneumati tō hagiō. Mēchanē is a machine 'for lifting weights', a crane (LSJ). Ignatius pictures a building site: the believers are 'stones of the Father's temple', the cross is the crane that lifts them, the Holy Spirit is the rope, faith is the hoist (Greek anagōgeus, 'one that brings up', LSJ; Lake: 'windlass'), and love is the road up.

The picture grows from the New Testament's living stones: 'you are being built up, as stones that live, into a spiritual house' (1 Peter 2:5), and 'it is growing up as a temple that is holy in the Lord' (Ephesians 2:21). What Ignatius adds is the machine. The church does not climb by itself; the cross lifts it.
orig: ἡ μηχανὴ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (hē mēchanē Iēsou Christou)

a: God-bearers and temple-bearers, Christ-bearers, bearers of holy things
p: Ignatius gives the Ephesians his own name: they too are God-bearers.
b: Greek theophoroi kai naophoroi, christophoroi, hagiophoroi. All four words end in -phoros, 'carrying', like Ignatius's second name Theophorus (1:0). The Ephesians carry God, his temple and Christ within them; Paul says 'your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you' (1 Corinthians 6:19). Greek synodoi, 'fellow travelers' (LSJ), sets the scene: a company on the road together. Chapter 9's page has a guess, labeled as Claude's, about the picture behind the words.
orig: θεοφόροι καὶ ναοφόροι, χριστοφόροι, ἁγιοφόροι (theophoroi kai naophoroi, christophoroi, hagiophoroi)

a: pray without a break
p: Paul's command, word for word in the Greek.
b: Greek adialeiptōs proseuchesthe, the words of 1 Thessalonians 5:17, which Lake prints in the margin: 'Pray without a break.' Ignatius applies it to praying for outsiders, 'the rest of humanity', as 1 Timothy 2:1 asks prayer 'for all people'. The pagans may still repent; Christians are to win them by their deeds before their words.

a: Against their anger, be gentle
p: Five short commands, in the spirit of the Sermon on the Mount.
b: Each line sets the outsiders' sin against the Christian's answer: anger and gentleness, boasting and humility, insults and prayer, error and firm faith, savagery and mildness. The thought is Jesus' 'pray for the people who persecute you' (Matthew 5:44) and Paul's 'Pay no one back evil for evil' (Romans 12:17). 'Gentle' is the word of 'Blessed are the gentle' (Matthew 5:5). Lake's margin points to Colossians 1:23 for the firm faith.

a: no weed of the devil
p: A picture from Jesus' parable of the weeds sown among the wheat.
b: Greek tou diabolou botanē, 'a plant of the devil'. In Jesus' parable the enemy 'sowed weeds over the top of the wheat' (Matthew 13:25), and 'any plant that was not planted by my heavenly Father will be uprooted' (Matthew 15:13). Ignatius has used the farming picture already: the false teachers wanted to 'sow' their teaching (9:1).

a: The last times are here
p: Ignatius believed the end was near, as the New Testament writers did.
b: Greek eschatoi kairoi, 'last times', with no verb. 1 John 2:18 says, 'it is the last hour', and Hebrews 1:2 that 'At the end of these days he has spoken to us in a Son'. Ignatius draws the same lesson: fear God's patience, which is giving time to repent (2 Peter 3:9), so that it does not become judgment. 'Either ... or ...: one of the two' leaves the motive open, fear or love, so long as one is found in Christ.

a: the pearls of the spirit
p: Ignatius wears his prison chains like a string of pearls.
b: Greek tous pneumatikous margaritas, 'the spiritual pearls'. Rich women of the time wore strings of pearls. Ignatius wears chains, and he counts them his jewels, the sign that he is Christ's. Paul calls himself 'the prisoner of Christ Jesus' (Ephesians 3:1) and says, 'My chains are now seen for what they are, chains for Christ' (Philippians 1:13). Ignatius hopes to 'rise again' in them: the chains lead to death, and death to the resurrection.

a: the Christians of Ephesus
p: A name rare in the New Testament, which Ignatius uses freely.
b: Greek tōn Christianōn. The name appears only three times in the New Testament (Acts 11:26, at Antioch, Ignatius's own city; Acts 26:28; 1 Peter 4:16). Ignatius uses it freely; in his letter to Rome he asks prayer that he may not only be called a Christian but be found one (Ignatius to the Romans 3:2).

a: You are the road that those being killed on their way to God pass along
t: Ephesus, the road of the martyrs
p: Prisoners bound for Rome passed through Ephesus, as Paul did.
b: Greek parodos este tōn eis theon anairoumenōn. Ephesus lay on the road from the East to Rome. Paul, on his last journey to Jerusalem, called the Ephesian elders to Miletus and told them, 'you will see my face no more' (Acts 20:25). Ignatius is now on the same kind of road, and he takes comfort that martyrs before him passed this way.

a: You share the mysteries with Paul
p: A word from the mystery religions: they and Paul share the same secret rites.
b: Greek Paulou symmystai, 'fellow initiates of Paul'. A symmystēs is 'one who is initiated with others' (LSJ), a word used in inscriptions of members of the mystery cults. Ignatius borrows it to say the Ephesians share with Paul in the mystery of Christ, which Paul himself made a theme of his letter to them (Ephesians 3:3-9). Ephesus had been Paul's home for more than two years (Acts 19:10). 'Given a good witness' (Greek memartyrēmenou) is the passive of Hebrews 11:2 and 11:39, for the faithful people of old whom God approved; by itself it does not mean 'martyred'. Since Ignatius names Paul right after 'those being killed on their way to God' and prays to walk 'in his tracks', a reader may ask whether Paul's death is in view as well, the question the note at 1 Clement 5:4 takes up for the active form of the verb. Here the passive alone does not settle it.

a: when I reach God
p: Ignatius's own phrase for his death as a martyr: 'reaching' God.
b: Greek hotan theou epitychō, 'when I attain God' (Lake: 'when I shall attain to God'). The verb means to hit a target, to obtain what one aims at. The Plain English Translation says 'reach' every time, so readers can follow the thread through the letters (1:2 'reach the goal'; Ignatius to the Romans 1:2; 2:1; 4:1). For Ignatius death in the arena is not loss but arrival.

a: In every letter he remembers you
p: What does Ignatius mean, since Paul names Ephesus in only some of his letters?
b: Greek en pasē epistolē mnēmoneuei hymōn. Paul mentions Ephesus or Ephesians in 1 Corinthians 15:32 and 16:8, 1 Timothy 1:3, 2 Timothy 1:18 and 4:12, as well as in the letter to them (Ephesians 1:1; the words 'in Ephesus' are missing from some of the oldest manuscripts there). 'Every letter' is more than that, and Ignatius may be speaking loosely, out of warm feeling. What the verse does show is that he knew Paul as a writer of letters. That he knew several of them rests on the rest of his letter: its greeting borrows the language of Ephesians 1 (see the note at 1:0), and Lake's margin sets 1 Corinthians beside 16:1 and 18:1 and Romans beside 8:2, 18:2 and 20:2.
r: Ephesians 1:1; 1 Corinthians 15:32; 1 Corinthians 16:8; 1 Timothy 1:3; 2 Timothy 1:18; 2 Timothy 4:12

a: the thanksgiving to God
p: Greek eucharistia: the word that became 'Eucharist'. Here probably the church's meal.
b: Greek eis eucharistian theou. The noun means 'thanksgiving', and it became the name 'Eucharist'. The Plain English Translation says 'the thanksgiving' everywhere, as in the Didache (Didache 9:1), so the reader sees the one Greek word and the site does not choose between 'Eucharist', 'Lord's Supper' and 'Communion'. Lake translates 'to give thanks', with the note: 'It is probable that there is here an allusion to the Eucharist.' The call to meet 'more often' fits that: the church's thanksgiving was its gathering. See the note at 20:2.

a: the powers of Satan are pulled down
p: The church's gathering is a battle in which Satan loses.
b: Greek kathairountai hai dynameis tou Satana. For Ignatius the church's meeting is not only a duty but a fight in the unseen world: when Christians gather 'in one place often', Satan's powers fall, and 13:2 adds that peace ends 'every war among those in heaven and those on earth'. Paul too speaks of a wrestling match 'against the rulers, against the authorities' (Ephesians 6:12) and of weapons with 'the power to tear down strongholds' (2 Corinthians 10:4).

a: they are God
p: A startling phrase: faith and love joined together 'are God'.
b: Greek ta de dyo en henotēti genomena theos estin, 'the two, having come into unity, is God'. Ignatius does not mean that faith and love are a second God. The nearest New Testament line is 'God is love' (1 John 4:8): where faith and love are joined, God himself is present. Lake translates 'it is God'. 'The end' (Greek telos) is also 'the goal', the word of 1 Timothy 1:5, which Lake prints in the margin: 'the goal of this order is love'.

a: No one who claims faith sins
p: A flat statement, like 1 John 3:6, and Ignatius explains it himself.
b: Greek oudeis pistin epangellomenos hamartanei, 'no one professing faith sins'. The verb is the plain present, and the Plain English Translation leaves it as flat as the Greek, as the site's 1 John does: 'Anyone who remains in him does not sin' (1 John 3:6). Ignatius gives his own point in the next lines: a profession is shown true by what it does ('The tree shows itself by its fruit'), and what counts is being 'found in the power of faith to the end'.
orig: οὐδεὶς πίστιν ἐπαγγελλόμενος ἁμαρτάνει (oudeis pistin epangellomenos hamartanei)

a: The tree shows itself by its fruit
p: Jesus' saying from Matthew 12:33, in Ignatius's own words.
b: Greek phaneron to dendron apo tou karpou autou. Lake's margin gives Matthew 12:33. The thought is Jesus': 'You can tell a tree by its fruit' (Matthew 12:33). Ignatius's Greek is different (phaneron, 'plain, evident', where Matthew has 'is known'), so the Plain English Translation gives his own form. It may be a saying remembered rather than read, a common thing in these writers.

a: who spoke, and it came to be
t: He spoke, and it came to be
p: The creating word of the Psalms: Christ the Teacher speaks, and the world exists.
b: Greek hos eipen, kai egeneto. Lake's margin points to the Greek Psalms and to Judith. The site's Psalm 33:9, from the Hebrew, reads, 'For he said it, and it was'; Judith sings, 'for you spoke, and they came to be' (Judith 16:14; Judith is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles). Ignatius gives the creating word to Christ, 'the one Teacher', as John does: 'In the beginning was the Word' (John 1:1). His point is that Christ's words were deeds, and even his silence was work.

a: hear his quiet
p: Ignatius pairs the word of Jesus with his silence.
b: Greek tēs hēsychias autou akouein. 'Quiet' (Greek hēsychia) is kept apart from 'silence' (sigē), as Ignatius keeps them. The one who 'truly possesses Jesus' word' hears more than the words: he hears what Jesus did without speaking, his patience before his accusers (Mark 14:61; 1 Peter 2:23), and God's hidden work (19:1, 'done in God's quiet'). Ignatius links this to the quiet overseer (6:1).

a: so that we may be his temples
p: Paul's teaching that believers are God's temple, in the plural.
b: Greek hina ōmen autou naoi. Lake's margin gives 1 Corinthians 3:16: 'Do you not know that you are God's temple, and that the Spirit of God lives in you?' Ignatius makes the temple plural, each believer a temple, as in 1 Corinthians 6:19, and adds that God will 'appear before our faces'.

a: those who ruin households will not inherit the kingdom of God
p: Paul's warning from 1 Corinthians 6:9-10, with one word changed.
b: Lake's margin gives 1 Corinthians 6:9-10, whose site wording is 'Do not be deceived ... will not inherit the kingdom of God'. Ignatius keeps Paul's frame and puts one word in place of Paul's list: oikophthoroi, 'those who ruin a house' (LSJ: 'one who ruins a house, a prodigal' and 'seducer, adulterer'). The point of 16:2 is the comparison: if those who wreck a family in the flesh lose the kingdom, how much worse is one who wrecks the faith, God's household.

a: the fire that cannot be put out
t: The fire that cannot be put out
p: Jesus' words for the judgment of Gehenna.
b: Greek eis to pyr to asbeston, the phrase of Mark 9:43: 'into Gehenna, into the fire that cannot be put out'. Ignatius applies it to the false teacher and to 'anyone who listens to him'. The warning shows how seriously he took teaching about Christ: it was not a matter of opinion but of life and death.
orig: τὸ πῦρ τὸ ἄσβεστον (to pyr to asbeston)

a: the Lord received perfumed oil on his head
p: Ignatius reads the woman's anointing of Jesus as a gift to the whole church.
b: Greek myron elaben epi tēs kephalēs autou ho kyrios. Lake's margin gives Matthew 26:7, where a woman 'poured it over his head', and John 12:3, where 'the smell of the oil filled the house'. Ignatius makes a picture of it: the perfume on Christ's head breathes 'incorruption' over the church, as Paul says that God 'spreads the scent of knowing him in every place' (2 Corinthians 2:14). Against it stands 'the foul smell' of the teaching of 'the ruler of this age'.

a: the ruler of this age
p: Ignatius's name for the devil, built on Paul's 'the rulers of this age'.
b: Greek tou archontos tou aiōnos toutou. Paul speaks of 'the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing' (1 Corinthians 2:6), who did not know God's hidden wisdom: 'None of the rulers of this age has known it' (1 Corinthians 2:8). John's Gospel has 'this world's ruler' (John 12:31). Ignatius uses the singular for Satan, and in 19:1 he builds on Paul's thought that the ruler did not know God's plan.
orig: τοῦ ἄρχοντος τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου (tou archontos tou aiōnos toutou)

a: the knowledge of God, which is Jesus Christ
p: Greek gnōsis, 'knowledge': not yet the 'knowledge' of the later Gnostic groups.
b: Greek theou gnōsin, ho estin Iēsous Christos. Ignatius's 'knowledge' is a person: knowing God is knowing Jesus Christ, as in John 17:3 and 2 Corinthians 4:6. The word later became the banner of groups called Gnostics, who claimed a secret knowledge; Ignatius's use is the ordinary one of the New Testament.

a: a stumbling block to those who do not believe
p: Ignatius strings together Paul's words on the cross from 1 Corinthians 1.
b: Lake's margin gives Galatians 5:11 and 1 Corinthians 1:20. Paul preached 'Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles' (1 Corinthians 1:23), and asked, 'Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age?' (1 Corinthians 1:20). Ignatius keeps two of the three questions in the site's wording and adds a third of his own about 'those who are called people of understanding'. 'The lowliest servant' is the word of 8:1.

a: our God, Jesus the Christ
p: Ignatius's fullest statement of who Jesus is, in a creed-like sentence.
b: Greek ho gar theos hēmōn Iēsous ho Christos. The verse is a small creed: conceived, born, baptized, suffered. The Catholic Encyclopedia lists 'the Incarnation (Ephesians 18)' among the teachings it finds in the letters. 'Of the seed of David' is the phrase of John 7:42 ('from David's seed'), Romans 1:3 and 2 Timothy 2:8, all of which Lake prints in the margin. Ignatius holds both sides together: 'of the seed of David and of the Holy Spirit', a true descendant of David and conceived by the Spirit, as Luke 1:35 and Matthew 1:20 tell it.
orig: ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦς ὁ Χριστὸς (ho theos hēmōn Iēsous ho Christos)

a: was carried in the womb by Mary
p: Greek ekyophorēthē: Mary truly carried him for nine months.
b: Greek ekyophorēthē hypo Marias, 'was carried in the womb by Mary'. Lake translates 'was conceived', but the verb names the whole pregnancy. Against teachers who said Christ only seemed to have a body, Ignatius stresses a real mother and a real birth. In his letter to Smyrna he says Christ was 'truly born of a virgin' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1).

a: so that through his suffering he might purify the water
p: Christ's baptism made the water of Christian baptism holy.
b: Greek hina tō pathei to hydōr katharisē, 'that by the suffering he might cleanse the water'. Lake translates 'that by himself submitting he might purify the water', with the footnote: 'Or perhaps "by his suffering"; but the allusion seems to be to the Baptism, not to the Passion.' The Greek word pathos is the one Ignatius uses for Christ's suffering on the cross (20:1), so the Plain English Translation keeps 'suffering'. Either way the thought is that Jesus, who had no sin, was baptized not to be made clean but to make the water clean for those baptized after him (compare Matthew 3:13-15). Later church writers developed the idea; see the topic Baptism and the card at Matthew 3.

a: escaped the notice of the ruler of this age
p: God's great acts were done in secret, so the devil did not see them coming.
b: Greek elathen ton archonta tou aiōnos toutou. Ignatius builds on Paul: 'None of the rulers of this age has known it. For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory' (1 Corinthians 2:8). Three things escaped the devil's notice: Mary's virginity, her giving birth, and the Lord's death. Paul too speaks of 'the plan of the mystery, kept hidden from the ages in God' (Ephesians 3:9).

a: three mysteries to be shouted aloud
p: Greek mystēria kraugēs: secrets done in silence, meant to be shouted.
b: Greek tria mystēria kraugēs, 'three mysteries of a cry'. Lake translates 'Three mysteries of a cry'; the sense is debated. The Plain English Translation takes it as a paradox: things done 'in God's quiet' that are meant to be cried aloud, as Jesus said, 'Whatever you hear in your ear, shout it from the rooftops' (Matthew 10:27). Kraugē is a loud cry, the word of Hebrews 5:7, where Jesus 'cried out loudly'. The genitive could also mean 'mysteries that cry out', mysteries that by their nature proclaim themselves.

a: Mary's virginity
p: Ignatius names the virgin birth as a fact his readers know.
b: Greek hē parthenia Marias kai ho toketos autēs, 'Mary's virginity and her giving birth'. Ignatius names the virgin birth as a fact his readers know, early in the second century, as Matthew 1:18-25 and Luke 1:26-38 tell it. The verse names her virginity and her giving birth as two hidden mysteries, side by side; it does not say how the one bears on the other. Whether Mary stayed a virgin in giving birth and afterward are later questions on which the churches differ, and the verse does not raise them (see the card at Matthew 1:25).

a: How, then, were they shown to the ages?
p: The Greek verb has no stated subject: the three mysteries, or Christ.
b: Greek pōs oun ephanerōthē tois aiōsin, 'how then was it (or he) made manifest to the ages?' The verb is singular and has no subject of its own. Greek often puts a singular verb with a neuter plural subject, so the subject can be the 'three mysteries' of 19:1, and the Plain English Translation reads it that way. Lake ('How then was he manifested to the world?') and Roberts and Donaldson take the subject to be Christ. Either way the answer is the star. The spec box on chapter 19's page depends on the first reading.
orig: πῶς οὖν ἐφανερώθη τοῖς αἰῶσιν (pōs oun ephanerōthē tois aiōsin)

a: A star blazed in the sky, outshining all the stars
p: Ignatius retells Matthew's star as a light that outshone the whole sky.
b:
Matthew's magi say, "We saw his star at its rising, and we have come to bow down to him." (Matthew 2:2), and later 'the star they had seen at its rising was going in front of them' (Matthew 2:9). Matthew does not say how bright it was. Ignatius goes further: the star outshone all the others, even the sun and moon, and they became its 'choir'. The picture recalls Joseph's dream: 'the sun, the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me!' (Genesis 37:9).

Lake's footnote says the metaphor of the choir 'is probably from the chorus or choir which gathered round the altar in heathen ceremonial, and sang a sacrificial hymn'. Ignatius's point is that all creation honored Christ. Whether he simply retold Matthew in the grand style or knew a fuller form of the story, the passage alone cannot tell.

a: all magic was undone
p: The birth of Christ breaks the power of magic and the old kingdom of evil.
b: Greek elyeto pasa mageia. The word for 'magic', mageia, belongs to the same family as 'magi' (Greek magoi), and the passage follows the star of Matthew 2, which led the magi to the child: once the star appeared, 'all magic was undone'. Magic was common in Ephesus: Acts tells how many believers there burned their books of magic (Acts 19:18-19). 'Every chain of evil' and 'the old kingdom' are the devil's rule, which ends as God is 'made known in a human way'.

a: the newness of everlasting life
p: Paul's 'life that is new', from Romans 6:4.
b: Greek eis kainotēta aidiou zōēs, 'for newness of everlasting life'. Lake's margin gives Romans 6:4, where the site says, 'we also might walk in a life that is new'. 'Newness' is a thread in this chapter: the star's 'newness' was astonishing (19:2), and in 20:1 Christ is 'the new man'.

a: the undoing of death was being prepared
p: All creation was stirred, because God was preparing to destroy death.
b: Greek dia to meletasthai thanatou katalysin. With the birth of Christ the plan to end death was under way, and 'everything was stirred up'. The thought is Paul's: 'The last enemy to be brought to an end is death' (1 Corinthians 15:26), and Hebrews 2:14, that by his death Christ could 'make powerless the one who wields the might of death'.

a: the second little book
t: A second letter that never came
p: Ignatius planned to write again; no genuine second letter is known.
b: Greek en tō deuterō biblidiō. Lake's footnote: 'This second book was either never written, or at all events is not extant in the genuine recension: but a later editor has supplied a "second epistle to the Ephesians" which is undoubtedly not genuine.' Ignatius was soon moved on: from Troas he wrote to Polycarp of 'my sudden sailing from Troas to Neapolis' (To Polycarp 8, Lake's English), and the Catholic Encyclopedia speaks of 'a hurried departure'.
orig: ἐν τῷ δευτέρῳ βιβλιδίῳ (en tō deuterō biblidiō)

a: the new man Jesus Christ
p: Ignatius calls Christ himself 'the new man'.
b: Greek ton kainon anthrōpon Iēsoun Christon. Paul uses the same Greek, kainos anthrōpos, for the church: Christ created 'one new humanity out of the two', Jews and Gentiles (Ephesians 2:15); and believers 'put on the new self' (Ephesians 4:24). Ignatius gives the title to Christ himself, the beginning of the new human race, as Paul calls him 'The last Adam' (1 Corinthians 15:45).

a: by name
p: Lake calls ex onomatos 'a strange phrase'.
b: Greek ex onomatos. Lake's footnote: 'Or possibly, as Lightfoot thinks, ex onomatos means "every individual of you." It is in any case a strange phrase.' Lake's own English says 'in grace from his name'. The Plain English Translation keeps the plain words and lets the reader see the puzzle. Lake adds of the whole sentence that his translation 'appears to be the only possible translation. But the text is not improbably corrupt'; see the variants on this verse.

a: the Son of Man and Son of God
t: Son of Man and Son of God
p: Both titles side by side: one person, truly human and truly divine.
b: Greek tō huiō anthrōpou kai huiō theou. In the Gospels 'the Son of Man' is Jesus' own title for himself, drawn from Daniel 7:13. Ignatius uses it beside 'Son of God' to name both sides of Christ, as he did in 7:2: 'in the flesh ... of David's family', and the Son of God.
orig: τῷ υἱῷ ἀνθρώπου καὶ υἱῷ θεοῦ (tō huiō anthrōpou kai huiō theou)

a: the medicine of immortality
p: The one bread is a medicine against death. Churches read it differently.
b:
Greek hena arton klōntes, hos estin pharmakon athanasias, antidotos tou mē apothanein. Pharmakon is a drug, healing or harmful (LSJ). The picture ties back to the 'one doctor' of 7:2: the doctor's medicine is the bread broken in the church. Jesus said, 'If someone eats from this bread, he will live forever' (John 6:51).

The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes this verse for the Eucharist as the pledge of eternal life: we 'break the one bread that provides the medicine of immortality, the antidote for death' (paragraph 1405). A Lutheran calendar of the Missouri Synod says Ignatius stressed 'the reality of Christ's bodily presence in the Lord's Supper'. Churches that see the Supper as a memorial read 'medicine' as a picture of Christ received by faith. Whether Christ's body and blood are present in the bread is the card at Matthew 26:26; whether John 6 speaks of the Supper is the card at John 6; and whether the Supper is a sacrifice is the card at Hebrews 10.

a: breaking one bread
p: The one loaf as a sign of one church, as in 1 Corinthians 10:17.
b: Greek hena arton klōntes. 'Break bread' is the phrase of Acts 2:42, 2:46 and 20:7. 'One' bread is Paul's point in 1 Corinthians 10:17: 'Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body.' For Ignatius one bread goes with one overseer and one council of elders: the unity of the church is seen at the table.

a: I am a life in exchange for you
p: Greek antipsychon: Ignatius offers his life on their behalf.
b: Greek antipsychon hymōn egō. The word means 'given for life' or 'giving one's own life for another's' (LSJ). 4 Maccabees uses it of the martyrs: 'They became, as it were, a life in exchange for the nation's sin' (4 Maccabees 17:22). Ignatius means his coming death is offered for the church, as he said in 8:1. Lake translates 'May my soul be given for yours'. Ignatius does not claim his death takes away their sins, which only Christ's does; he speaks the language of devotion.

a: Polycarp
p: Ignatius's host in Smyrna, later its famous martyr.
b: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, received Ignatius there. Eusebius says Polycarp had been 'entrusted with the episcopate of the church of Smyrna by those who had seen and heard the Lord' (Church History 3.36.1). Later Polycarp sent copies of Ignatius's letters to Philippi: 'As you asked, we have sent you the letters of Ignatius, the ones he sent us, and the others we had here with us' (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2). His own death is told in the Martyrdom of Polycarp.

a: the last of the faithful there
p: Ignatius calls himself the least of the believers of his own church.
b: Greek eschatos ōn tōn ekei pistōn, 'being last of the faithful there'. 'Last' is humility, as Paul calls himself 'one born at the wrong time' and 'the least of the apostles' (1 Corinthians 15:8-9). Lake says one of the aims running through the letters is to secure the future 'of his own church in Antioch by persuading other communities to send helpers'. The letter to Rome asks the same prayer for 'the church in Syria' (Ignatius to the Romans 9:1).
